raw_response:
I am a seventy-year-old man, and I have worked this land since I was twenty. Six mu is not much—my father had the same, and his father before him—but I learned a great deal at the agricultural college in Shijiazhuang, and I have spent fifty years watching how these fields respond. My wife and I are the only ones left in the household now. Our son works in Beijing and sends money when he can, but I do not count on it. I must run this farm with my own cash, and at my age, I cannot carry heavy loads or work long days in the sun. I hire labor for transplanting and harvest, and I pay close attention to the returns on every yuan I spend.

It is early March now. The soil is just thawing. I have six mu, and I think of it as three main plots plus two small beds by the well. This year I am keeping my rotation: spring cabbage on the east plot, maize on the south plot, and spinach in the small beds near the house. I also keep a strip of chili peppers and a row of kidney beans for the market in Quzhou town and for our own table. I do not grow wheat anymore—at my age, the harvest is too exhausting and the margins are too thin. Vegetables give better cash returns per mu, though they demand more labor and more careful water management.

For the spring cabbage on 1.5 mu, I started the seedlings in my small plastic tunnel in February. I will transplant in late March. Cabbage is a heavy feeder, and I know from soil tests I did two years ago that my nitrogen is moderate but phosphorus is a bit low. I will apply a base dressing of 12 kg N, 5 kg P₂O₅, and 6 kg K₂O per mu as compound fertilizer before transplanting. Then at the rosette stage, I will topdress with another 6 kg N per mu as urea. That gives me 18 kg N per mu total—slightly below the textbook optimum of 22 kg, but I am cash-constrained and I supplement with two cartloads of composted chicken manure per mu, which my neighbor sells me cheap. I will irrigate four times: right after transplanting, at rosette, at heading, and once more before harvest in mid-June. I need to watch for cabbage worms and downy mildew, so I will spray Bacillus thuringiensis once and a fungicide if the spring is wet. I expect about 4,000 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

The maize on 2 mu I will plant around April 15 with an early-maturing hybrid variety, Zhengdan 958. I have used this variety for ten years. It is reliable. I will band-apply compound fertilizer at planting giving me 10 kg N, 4 kg P, and 4 kg K per mu, then topdress with urea at jointing for another 5 kg N per mu. So 15 kg N per mu total. Maize does not need as much irrigation as vegetables in this county, but if May is dry I will run the pump twice—once at jointing and once at tasseling. I should get 450 kg per mu. I will hire a small tractor for plowing because I cannot handle the walk-behind tractor for long anymore.

The chili peppers on 0.8 mu I will transplant in early May, after the last frost risk. I grow a local hybrid that the buyers at the county market prefer. Chili needs potassium for fruit quality, so I target 12 kg N, 5 kg P, and 10 kg K per mu, split into base, flowering, and first fruit-set applications. I will irrigate four times, but I am careful not to over-water at flowering or I get blossom drop. This crop is labor-intensive—I will hire two women from the village for the picking in July through September. I expect 300 kg per mu of fresh chili.

The kidney beans on 0.5 mu are partly for market and partly for our own eating. I will direct-seed in mid-April. I keep my own seed from last year, so seed cost is low. I apply a modest 8 kg N, 4 kg P, and 5 kg K per mu, mostly as base dressing. Two irrigations and minimal pesticide—maybe one herbicide spray early. Yield should be around 250 kg per mu.

Spinach on 0.7 mu is my quick cash crop. I sow the first batch in early March under a thin plastic cover, harvest by early May, then sow a fall batch in September. For the spring crop, I apply 10 kg N, 3 kg P, and 4 kg K per mu, with one side-dressing of urea. Three irrigations. Spinach is forgiving, and I can get 1,200 kg per mu per crop. The fall crop uses the same bed after I clear the spring spinach.

Fall cabbage on 0.5 mu I will transplant in late July, after the spring cabbage land is cleared and I have added compost. This is my storage cabbage for winter market and home use. I apply 15 kg N, 6 kg P, and 8 kg K per mu in two splits, irrigate three times, and harvest in November before hard frost. Expected yield 3,500 kg per mu.

I must be careful with cash. My total input budget this year is about 4,200 yuan. I could push for higher yields with more fertilizer, but at seventy, I prefer steady, known outcomes. If I lose a crop to weather or pests, I cannot make up for it with extra labor. I also need to keep 1,000 yuan in reserve for medicine or pump repairs. The hired labor will cost me roughly 2,800 yuan across the season—transplanting cabbage and chili, picking chili, and harvesting cabbage. That is my biggest expense after fertilizer. I have the well, and irrigation water is metered, so I watch every pumping hour.
